questions.q: A grave inscription read, “I was important, this was the illusion.” What does the article say produces this illusion?
options: Living far from other people
Not quite. The article says: Using God’s blessings without acknowledging their Giver, until one feels he owns the world he has built.
Having too little education
Not quite. The article says: Using God’s blessings without acknowledging their Giver, until one feels he owns the world he has built.
Using God’s blessings without acknowledging their Giver, until one feels he owns the world he has built
Yes. Old age and death show it never belonged to him.
Being praised too much by others
Not quite. The article says: Using God’s blessings without acknowledging their Giver, until one feels he owns the world he has built.
questions.rationale: “He does not acknowledge the Bestower of all these blessings. As a result, he consciously or unconsciously comes to feel that he himself was the owner of the world he had created for himself.”

questions.q: A man dying young told his visitors, “Don’t think about me; think about yourself.” What did he want them to realise?
options: A healthy body is a gift from God that can be taken back at any time, so it calls for gratitude
Right. Acknowledging the gift is the test of life.
That youth is the best time of life
Not quite. The article says: A healthy body is a gift from God that can be taken back at any time, so it calls for gratitude.
That visitors tire the sick
Not quite. The article says: A healthy body is a gift from God that can be taken back at any time, so it calls for gratitude.
That illness can be avoided by care
Not quite. The article says: A healthy body is a gift from God that can be taken back at any time, so it calls for gratitude.
questions.rationale: “Be grateful for having a healthy body. You eat, you drink, and you walk on the ground. All these things are God’s blessings.”

questions.q: What attitude of the Japanese after 1945 does the article credit for their rapid progress?
options: A realistic willingness to share the blame and not let grievance rule their lives
Yes. “We were quits, and now we are friends.”
Reliance on rich natural resources
Not quite. The article says: A realistic willingness to share the blame and not let grievance rule their lives.
A determination to take revenge
Not quite. The article says: A realistic willingness to share the blame and not let grievance rule their lives.
A refusal to remember the war
Not quite. The article says: A realistic willingness to share the blame and not let grievance rule their lives.
questions.rationale: “This realistic attitude on the part of the Japanese has seen them through all kinds of adversity and brought them to extraordinary heights of progress.”

questions.q: Why, according to the article, does a readiness to admit one’s own fault end a quarrel?
options: It allows the courts to decide quickly
Not quite. The article says: Shouldering the blame softens the other side, so the dispute dies a natural death.
Shouldering the blame softens the other side, so the dispute dies a natural death
Well read. Blaming only the other makes it worse.
It makes the other side afraid
Not quite. The article says: Shouldering the blame softens the other side, so the dispute dies a natural death.
It proves the other side was right in everything
Not quite. The article says: Shouldering the blame softens the other side, so the dispute dies a natural death.
questions.rationale: “The very gesture of shouldering the blame softens up the other side, with the result that the dispute dies a natural death.”

questions.q: What does the article say remembrance of God really is?
options: A count of words on a rosary
Not quite. The article says: A feeling that wells up from the depths of the soul on discovering God – not a mere repetition of words.
A feeling that wells up from the depths of the soul on discovering God – not a mere repetition of words
Correct. It takes the form of words by itself.
A practice reserved for special nights
Not quite. The article says: A feeling that wells up from the depths of the soul on discovering God – not a mere repetition of words.
A fixed formula known to a few
Not quite. The article says: A feeling that wells up from the depths of the soul on discovering God – not a mere repetition of words.
questions.rationale: “Remembrance of God is not a mere repetition of words. Rather it is a feeling that wells up from the very depths of a man’s soul.”

questions.q: What formula does the article give for living with religious differences?
options: Merge all traditions into one
Not quite. The article says: “Follow one, respect all” – since removing differences is impossible.
“Follow one, respect all” – since removing differences is impossible
Yes. Live and let live.
Keep communities apart
Not quite. The article says: “Follow one, respect all” – since removing differences is impossible.
Leave the matter to the police
Not quite. The article says: “Follow one, respect all” – since removing differences is impossible.
questions.rationale: “The solution to the religious differences is to deal it with a simple formula of ‘follow one, respect all’. Trying to eliminate the differences is impossible and against the law of nature.”

questions.q: How does the article contrast provision in this life with the life after death?
options: Here God provides what is needed for the test; the life after depends entirely on one’s own actions
Right. “You will reap as you have sown.”
Neither can be known
Not quite. The article says: Here God provides what is needed for the test; the life after depends entirely on one’s own actions.
Both are provided without effort
Not quite. The article says: Here God provides what is needed for the test; the life after depends entirely on one’s own actions.
Both depend entirely on effort
Not quite. The article says: Here God provides what is needed for the test; the life after depends entirely on one’s own actions.
questions.rationale: “It is God’s responsibility to provide every one of us with the things that we need to go through this test… Our life after death depends entirely on our actions in this world.”

questions.q: A man cheated of his ancestral farmland went to the city and in time owned a factory. What does the article draw from this?
options: Loss can be a ladder to progress, if one keeps courage and uses one’s abilities
Yes. Another opportunity is always at hand.
Villages should be left behind
Not quite. The article says: Loss can be a ladder to progress, if one keeps courage and uses one’s abilities.
Farming is less rewarding than industry
Not quite. The article says: Loss can be a ladder to progress, if one keeps courage and uses one’s abilities.
Relatives should not be trusted
Not quite. The article says: Loss can be a ladder to progress, if one keeps courage and uses one’s abilities.
questions.rationale: “In this world there are so many opportunities that here even in loss there is some aspect of gain… provided he does not lose courage.”

questions.q: What is “superior morality,” in the article’s definition?
options: Being kind to those of one’s own group
Not quite. The article says: Keeping to good conduct in every situation, on one’s own principles, whatever others do.
Treating people as they treat you
Not quite. The article says: Keeping to good conduct in every situation, on one’s own principles, whatever others do.
Keeping to good conduct in every situation, on one’s own principles, whatever others do
Exactly. Not returning like for like.
Avoiding people who behave badly
Not quite. The article says: Keeping to good conduct in every situation, on one’s own principles, whatever others do.
questions.rationale: “Superior morality is not based on the reactions of others, but rather on one’s own higher principles and standards.”

questions.q: What does Maulana say about the relation between his reading and his writing?
options: He writes first and reads afterwards
Not quite. The article says: Writing should be the result of reading; it should not be the motive for reading.
Writing should be the result of reading; it should not be the motive for reading
Well read. His own writing is a by-product of study.
He reads only in order to write
Not quite. The article says: Writing should be the result of reading; it should not be the motive for reading.
The two are unrelated
Not quite. The article says: Writing should be the result of reading; it should not be the motive for reading.
questions.rationale: “An author’s work should be a result of their reading. Writing should not be the motivation for reading.”
